algorithms.name: Fields2Cover (F2C): headland generator, brute-force swath-angle generator with objectives, boustrophedon/snake/OR-tools route planner, Dubins/Reeds-Shepp CC path planner
algorithms.reference: G. Mier, J. Valente, S. de Bruin, 'Fields2Cover: An open-source coverage path planning library for unmanned agricultural vehicles', IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters 8(4):2166-2172, 2023, DOI 10.1109/LRA.2023.3248439 (venue/DOI from the repo README citation). Extended in Mier's 2026 WUR PhD thesis (DOI 10.18174/681452).
algorithms.category: Agricultural CPP library / route and swath optimisation (de-facto open-source standard)
algorithms.core_idea: Modular CPP pipeline: constant-width headland, swath generation that brute-forces the driving angle (default 1 degree step) against a swath objective (NSwath, NSwathModified, SwathLength, FieldCoverage, Overlaps), then swath ordering (boustrophedon, snake, spiral, or an OR-tools route optimiser in v2) and turn generation with continuous-curvature Dubins/Reeds-Shepp curves. Swaths are spaced deterministically at op_width. Execution uncertainty is not modelled; users handle it by setting op_width below the implement width (a fixed overlap).
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: (1) Install: PyPI 'fields2cover' 2.1.0 is an sdist only (I downloaded it). It builds with scikit-build-core and SWIG and needs GDAL and OR-tools. A fallback is to re-implement BruteForce plus the Overlaps and FieldCoverage objectives in shapely, about 100 lines. (2) Same fields: pass each field polygon (meta['polygon_enu']) to F2C. Use ConstHL with width 2w so the headland matches core.Field (H = 2w). Run BruteForce.generateBestSwaths with each objective at op_width = w, and also at w - 2m for the overlaps m that F2C users would actually set (5, 10, 30 cm). (3) Map back to our pipeline: convert the best angle theta* to meta['heading_deg'] (compass = 90 - theta in degrees) and rebuild core.Field so the DEM gradient is re-rotated. Set ys to the perpendicular offsets of the swath midpoints. Then run the same core.simulate (same Condition seeds, controller LQR-I/PP/Stanley/LQR, real RTK) and core.evaluate / exp_lib.overlap_ratio. (4) Path length and number of passes: take these from F2C's path planner (DubinsCurvesCC with our vehicle's r_min) for every method, ours included, so the turn and length metrics come from one shared tool. (5) Report three rows: F2C at its own angle; F2C at the real harvester heading (isolates the angle effect); and F2C+CE, where CE erosion h_k = w/2 - q*sigma_k is applied to F2C's swaths at theta*. This shows CE is a planner-agnostic certificate layer. (6) Avoid points collapsing at P=0: sweep F2C's only robustness knob (op_width) to draw its overlap vs P(no-miss) frontier, and mark where F2C's default and the oracle-tuned op_width land against CE's certified point.
algorithms.open_source_code: https://github.com/Fields2Cover/Fields2Cover (BSD-3, ~900 stars; verified via GitHub search); PyPI: fields2cover 2.1.0

algorithms.name: IRIS-U^2: inspection/coverage planning under execution uncertainty with Monte-Carlo statistical guarantees
algorithms.reference: S. D. Alpert, K. Solovey, I. Klein, O. Salzman, 'Inspection planning under execution uncertainty', IEEE Transactions on Robotics, vol. 41, pp. 2406-2423, 2025 (arXiv 2309.06113)
algorithms.category: Uncertainty-aware coverage planning with statistical (sampling-based) guarantees: the closest conceptual competitor
algorithms.core_idea: Extends the IRIS inspection planner. During an A*-style search over candidate plans, localisation and execution uncertainty is propagated by Monte-Carlo sampling of executions. Each point of interest gets an estimated coverage probability, and the planner returns confidence intervals on expected coverage, path length and collision probability. The intervals tighten as the number of MC samples m grows. Bounded-suboptimal variants trade compute for optimality. The guarantee holds only under the planner's own uncertainty model.
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: Implement it as 'model-based MC certification' (no public code found). (1) Planning-time model: the competitor only gets a model, never the true distribution. Use (a) our simulator with Condition parameters fitted by maximum likelihood or moment matching on the SAME n_cal calibration runs CE uses (fair data budget), and (b) a nominal model (prior-mean slip and roll compensation, Gaussian RTK with matched variance). (2) Candidate plans: margin lambda on a grid (core.plan with the same sig_fn) times a heading set, mirroring IRIS's search over plans. (3) For each candidate, run m = 100-500 rollouts of the model through core.simulate and core.evaluate. Estimate per-cell coverage probability (IRIS's POI view) and run-level P(no miss). Take a Clopper-Pearson lower bound at 1 - beta (beta = 0.05). Select the minimum-overlap candidate whose LCB is at least 1 - eps. Also report their expected-coverage CI, which is the analogue of CE-R. (4) Evaluate on the TRUE execution (different seeds and the real heavy-tailed RTK) with the same metrics. (5) The key experiments: with a well-specified model it is valid but costs m rollouts per candidate per field (report runtime against CE's single quantile). Under misspecification (Gaussian vs real RTK, LOBO/LODO shift, and CitrusFarm, where the model is our kinematic sim and the truth is real robot traces) its 'guarantee' should break while CE's holds, or both degrade and ACI recovers. This is the head-to-head a T-RO/RA-L reviewer will ask for.
algorithms.open_source_code: none found (GitHub search for IRIS-U2 / Salzman returned nothing)

algorithms.name: Side-to-side 3D coverage planning with numerical skip/overlap estimation and driving-angle selection (Hameed et al.)
algorithms.reference: I. A. Hameed, A. la Cour-Harbo, O. L. Osen, 'Side-to-side 3D coverage path planning approach for agricultural robots to minimize skip/overlap areas between swaths', Robotics and Autonomous Systems 76:36-45, 2016 (ScienceDirect PII S0921889015002973; DOI unverified). Related: I. A. Hameed, 'Intelligent coverage path planning for agricultural robots and autonomous machines on three-dimensional terrain', J. Intelligent & Robotic Systems 74:965-983, 2014, DOI 10.1007/s10846-013-9834-6; Hameed, Bochtis, Sorensen, Jensen, Larsen, 'Optimized driving direction based on a three-dimensional field representation', Computers and Electronics in Agriculture 91:145-153, 2013.
algorithms.category: Terrain-aware (3D) agricultural CPP that explicitly minimises skip/overlap
algorithms.core_idea: Projecting a 2D plan onto sloped terrain stretches the surface distance between adjacent paths, and machine roll shrinks the effective implement width, which together cause skips on slopes. Two parts: (i) a numerical estimator of total skip and overlap area for a given driving angle on a DEM, used to choose the angle with the least skip/overlap; (ii) a side-to-side placement that spaces each new path from the previous one by the working width measured on the terrain surface, giving zero skips under nominal (perfect) tracking. The reported saving is 2-14% of field area (search snippet).
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: (1) Evaluator fix, needed for fairness and applied to all methods: core.evaluate currently uses a horizontal footprint of width w regardless of slope. Add the 3D projection: horizontal half-width = (w/2)*cos(atan(g_y(x, y_k+o))), with g_y from Field.gy. Otherwise terrain-aware planners get no credit. (2) Angle selection: for each heading in 0-179 degrees at 1 degree, rebuild core.Field with that heading. Compute Hameed's skip+overlap estimate for the nominal plan as the sum over pass pairs and x of max(0, gap_surface) plus overlap_surface, using the DEM, and keep the minimiser. (3) Side-to-side placement: replace the fixed-point step in core.plan with y_{k+1} = y_k + min over x in chord of w*cos(atan|g_y(x, y)|) (solved by 3-4 fixed-point iterations as in plan()). This yields zero skip under perfect tracking. (4) Execute with the same core.simulate and controllers. Expect P(no-miss) near 0 because it ignores execution noise. That is fine: it is the strongest deterministic terrain planner. Also report 'Hameed+CE', applying CE erosion on top of the side-to-side spacing. That variant also gives CE-A a physically grounded terrain term, which could rescue the CE-A vs CE-U story. (5) Optional variant: Plessen's 2026 terrain-following planner (arXiv 2601.00614, ICARSC 2026, adds a working height above terrain), cited as the newest 3D descendant.

algorithms.name: Online pass-to-pass replanning: track-spacing adaptation / sensor-driven online coverage (the as-driven-previous-pass reference)
algorithms.reference: V. Yordanova, B. Gips, 'Coverage path planning with track spacing adaptation for autonomous underwater vehicles', arXiv 2006.12896, 2020 (journal venue unverified); L. Paull, S. Saeedi, M. Seto, H. Li, 'Sensor-driven online coverage planning for autonomous underwater vehicles', IEEE/RSJ IROS 2012, pp. 2875-2880, DOI 10.1109/IROS.2012.6385838; journal follow-up: Paull et al., 'Sensor-driven area coverage for an autonomous fixed-wing UAV', IEEE Trans. Cybernetics, 2014 (details unverified)
algorithms.category: Online / feedback coverage replanning: the reviewer-obvious alternative to an offline certified margin
algorithms.core_idea: Instead of fixing all swaths offline, the next track's spacing is adapted online from what was actually achieved on the previous track. Yordanova and Gips move the overlap to the far edge of the sensor and recover from overestimated range in sea trials. Paull et al. keep a probabilistic coverage map from pose uncertainty and plan the next path to fill low-probability regions. In agriculture this corresponds to auto-steer 'pass-to-pass' and adaptive-curve guidance that follows the as-driven previous pass.
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: (1) Make core.simulate sequential over passes. For pass k+1 the controller's reference is no longer the straight line ys[k+1]. It becomes r_{k+1}(x) = yhat_k(x) + w - m, where yhat_k(x) is the MEASURED trajectory of pass k: ys_k + d + antenna roll term + RTK sample, i.e. exactly the 'meas' signal already computed. The true trajectory is never observed. Variant: a straight AB line at y_{k+1} = max over x of yhat_k(x) + w - m. (2) Margins: m = 0 (pure pass-to-pass), m = fixed 5/10 cm, and m = CE-calibrated on the online residual score S_online = sup_x (e_{k+1} - e_k^meas)/... ('Online+CE'), which shows CE is complementary. (3) Paull-style variant: keep a per-cell coverage probability by propagating RTK error variance through the footprint, and place the next pass so every cell of the previous pass's far edge has coverage probability of at least 1 - eps/K. (4) Metrics as usual; passes now emerge online, so report the number of passes, overlap and path length too. Expected finding to discuss honestly: online replanning removes most tracking-error accumulation, but it cannot remove measurement bias (RTK error, residual roll-compensation error), because it sees measured rather than true positions. It also produces curved passes (bad for row crops and later operations) and is impossible where passes are fixed by crop rows (harvest follows planted rows). CE's certificate covers what remains. If online wins on overlap in some regime, report it; hiding it would be fatal at Q1.

algorithms.name: Coverage path planning in belief space (localizability-aware lane planning)
algorithms.reference: R. Schirmer, P. Biber, C. Stachniss, 'Coverage path planning in belief space', IEEE ICRA 2019 (Bosch / Univ. Bonn)
algorithms.core_idea: Uses a map to predict localizability, i.e. the expected pose covariance, at every location. It then searches over parallel-lane (meander) coverage paths in belief space and picks lanes and orientations that keep the robot safe and well localised. Uncertainty enters planning through a predicted covariance, not through data-driven calibration.
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: Build a 'belief-space boustrophedon' as the model-based counterpart of CE-A. (1) Linearise the closed loop of core.simulate (state [d, psi, delta, int d]; gains from core._lqr_gains). Model three noise sources: OU slip process noise whose intensity grows with |g_y| from the DEM (k_s*0.35*g + OU rough); RTK measurement noise with variance from rtk_lateral(); and the antenna roll bias h*sin(roll)*(1-comp) with variance from comp's spread. (2) Propagate the discrete Lyapunov/Kalman covariance along each candidate lane to get P_k(x). (3) Spacing: y_{k+1} = y_k + w - z*sqrt(max_x(P_k(x) + P_{k+1}(x))), with z = Phi^{-1}(1 - eps/(K-1)) (Bonferroni over pairs) or z tuned to the run-level target via a Gaussian sup approximation. Pick the lane orientation by brute force over headings to minimise total overlap, mirroring Schirmer's search. (4) Execute and evaluate identically. This tests the reviewer's question directly: is a principled physics/covariance-based sigma map better than CE's data-calibrated one? Expect it to be valid when the linear-Gaussian model holds, but under-covering with heavy-tailed real RTK and soil variability (the CitrusFarm replay is the decisive test). Report it alongside CE-A, where CE can also calibrate its sigma map.
algorithms.open_source_code: none found (paper reports a C++/ROS implementation)

algorithms.name: H-CCPP: 3D hybrid coverage path planning for agricultural fields (tree-based exploration + Fields2Cover, inclination-aware, fixed GNSS buffer)
algorithms.reference: D. Pour Arab, M. Spisser, C. Essert, '3D hybrid path planning for optimized coverage of agricultural fields: A novel approach for wheeled robots', Journal of Field Robotics, 2025, DOI 10.1002/rob.22422 (volume/pages unverified)
algorithms.core_idea: Combines the authors' earlier tree-based exploration of coverage configurations with Fields2Cover's efficient swath and route generation. The multi-objective cost maximises covered area and minimises overlaps, non-working path length and travel time, and it accounts for the inclination of working trajectories to limit soil erosion and energy use. GNSS positioning error is handled with a fixed safety buffer around field boundaries and obstacles, a deterministic margin. 2D and 3D representations of 30 French fields were released as a dataset.
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: (1) Implement on top of the F2C adaptation (entry 1). Add a custom SGObjective = alpha*(1 - FieldCoverage) + beta*Overlaps + gamma*(non-working length from the F2C path planner) + kappa*(mean |longitudinal slope| along swaths, from Field.gx_map). Search headings with F2C BruteForce, and optionally the tree search over cell decompositions as in their method (unverified detail). (2) GNSS buffer: implement their fixed buffer as a constant inset b of the main area plus the corresponding fixed swath overlap. Set b by their rule if recoverable from the paper (value unverified), otherwise b = 95% quantile of the real RTK lateral error. Note that this is exactly the 'deterministic margin' category CE replaces, but now inside a published Q1 planner. (3) Execute the resulting swaths with core.simulate and score with the same metrics, plus path length. (4) Report 'H-CCPP+CE' too. (5) If their 30-field 2D/3D dataset can be downloaded (reachability unverified; ESS Open Archive / Wiley may be blocked), add it as an external benchmark.
algorithms.open_source_code: none found (searched GitHub and the web for H-CCPP)

algorithms.name: PAC (probably approximately correct) coverage under motion uncertainty
algorithms.reference: C. Das, A. Becker, T. Bretl, 'Probably approximately correct coverage for robots with uncertainty', 2011 (IEEE/RSJ venue and DOI unverified; PDF at Univ. Houston swarmcontrol site); see also C. Das, M.S. thesis 'Coverage for mobile robots with uncertainty', UIUC 2011
algorithms.category: Probabilistic-guarantee coverage (parametric chance constraint on covered fraction)
algorithms.core_idea: Under significant sensing and actuation uncertainty, full coverage is not guaranteed, so performance is defined as the probability 1-eps of covering a fraction 1-delta of the free space. A feedback policy (for example a square-wave or boustrophedon path with chosen spacing) is designed to meet (eps, delta) with minimal execution time. The thesis found passes parallel to the short axis performed better than the long axis. A later Paull et al. paper notes it assumes constant localisation error.
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: (1) Note that delta = 0 is exactly our P(no missed area) criterion, and delta > 0 links to CE-R. (2) Fit the parametric motion model PAC assumes, on the same calibration runs as CE: per-pass lateral error as a pass-level offset plus an AR(1)/Gauss-Markov process (fit with statsmodels on D from exp_lib.run). (3) Choose a uniform spacing s, or the equivalent lambda for core.plan, by MC under the fitted model so that P(covered fraction >= 1 - delta) >= 1 - eps, using a binary search on s. (4) Test both headings: the real harvester heading and the short-axis heading (Das's finding). (5) Evaluate on the true execution. It differs from our 'Gaussian chance constraint' baseline because it is a full published algorithm with a model of along-track correlation. It should be valid when the AR(1) model fits, and should fail with heavy tails and non-stationarity (slope-dependent slip). Present the delta-sweep curve against CE-R to avoid collapsed points.

algorithms.name: Deep-RL coverage path planning (frontier-map SAC agent; sim-to-real with wheel slip)
algorithms.reference: A. Jonnarth, J. Zhao, M. Felsberg, 'Learning coverage paths in unknown environments with deep reinforcement learning', ICML 2024, PMLR 235:22491-22508; follow-up A. Jonnarth, O. Johansson, (J. Zhao), M. Felsberg, 'Sim-to-real transfer of deep reinforcement learning agents for online coverage path planning', arXiv 2406.04920 (v3 2025, journal venue unverified). Agricultural DRL-CPP papers seen (Agronomy 2024 BL-DQN; PPO action-masking tractor agent) are in lower-tier or unverified venues.
algorithms.core_idea: An end-to-end RL agent (SAC with egocentric multi-scale frontier maps and a total-variation reward term that promotes complete coverage) plans continuous-control coverage paths online, including lawn-mowing coverage. The sim-to-real follow-up studies the gap from real kinematics and wheel slip and finds high inference frequency matters. There is no coverage guarantee.
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: Two options, with (B) recommended for a fair, tractable comparison. (A) Faithful: use rl-cpp's environment with the field polygon as a known map, mowing footprint w, our slip dynamics (DEM-driven, from core.simulate) and RTK noise injected into the agent's position observation. Train on the training fields and test on held-out fields. This is expensive, and the agent will not produce straight swaths. (B) DRL lane-offset policy on our pipeline: an episode is one field operation; at each pass boundary the state is (measured deviation statistics of pass k, DEM lateral-slope features of the next lane from core.pass_feature, remaining lateral width); the action is the next lane spacing; the reward is -overlap - C*1[missed area > 0]. Train SAC/PPO (stable-baselines3 from PyPI, optionally the rl-cpp network/reward ideas) inside core.simulate on training fields; test on test fields, under LOBO/LODO and controller shift. Report P(no-miss), E[missed], overlap and passes. Expected: competitive overlap in-distribution, but no certificate, with failures under shift. That is the 'learning vs certified' contrast Q1 reviewers ask for.
algorithms.open_source_code: https://github.com/arvijj/rl-cpp (official implementation; verified via GitHub search)

algorithms.name: 3D-terrain coverage path planning for arable farming (terrain decomposition + per-region direction optimisation)
algorithms.reference: J. Jin, L. Tang, 'Coverage path planning on three-dimensional terrain for arable farming', Journal of Field Robotics 28(3):424-440, 2011 (pre-2013 but the canonical 3D agricultural CPP; methodological details from secondary sources, so unverified); 2D precursor: Jin & Tang, Trans. ASABE 53(1):283-295, 2010
algorithms.core_idea: Classifies the field terrain into flat and sloped areas, decomposes the field accordingly, and in each region applies the most appropriate path-planning strategy and driving direction under a terrain-aware cost model. Secondary sources describe costs for headland turning and slope effects; the exact seed-curve and erosion terms are unverified.
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: (1) Decompose each field by DEM slope class: threshold |grad z| or k-means on (slope, aspect) from Field.gx_map/gy_map, then make the cells convex with F2C's boustrophedon/trapezoidal decomposition. (2) For each cell, brute-force the heading against a 3D cost: surface-projected skip+overlap (as in Hameed), headland turn count times turn cost, and cross-slope exposure. (3) Build one core.Field-like object per cell (its own rotation), simulate the passes per cell with core.simulate, and evaluate coverage of the union. This needs a small extension of core.evaluate to merge cell coverages on a common grid. (4) Report 'Jin-Tang' and 'Jin-Tang+CE'. It answers 'did you compare with a decomposition-based 3D planner?' and tests whether direction/decomposition alone reduces skips under execution noise. Probably not, which supports CE's thesis. Medium-low priority because it predates 2013 and the details are unverified.
algorithms.url: none (citation confirmed via secondary sources in search results)

algorithms.name: Soil2Cover: compaction-aware coverage path planning (SoilFlex + controlled traffic, built on Fields2Cover)
algorithms.reference: G. Mier, R. Velez, J. Valente, S. de Bruin, 'Soil2Cover: Coverage path planning minimizing soil compaction for sustainable agriculture', Precision Agriculture, 2025, DOI 10.1007/s11119-025-10250-4 (open access, PMC12134033)
algorithms.category: Agricultural CPP with agronomic objective (route/headland optimisation)
algorithms.core_idea: Optimises the swath order and headland routing so that wheel passes over each area are counted and the compaction effect is estimated with the SoilFlex soil-mechanics model under controlled-traffic principles. On 1000 fields it reduces route length by up to 4-6% and headland compaction by up to 30%, for single-crop and intercropping layouts.
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: Use it as a secondary-metric competitor, not a skip/overlap competitor. (1) Keep each method's swath set fixed (nominal, F2C, CE-U, ...). (2) Order swaths and build headland routes with F2C's OR-tools route planner and a compaction-aware cost (wheel-pass count per headland cell times a SoilFlex-style stress proxy; the exact SoilFlex parameters are in the paper). (3) Report path length, headland passes/compaction proxy and turn count for 'F2C route', 'Soil2Cover route' and 'Soil2Cover route on CE swaths'. This quantifies whether CE's extra swaths (more overlap means more passes) cost compaction and route length, and shows CE composes with route optimisers. Code location is unverified (likely inside or near the Fields2Cover repo); if unavailable, re-implement the pass-count cost in the OR-tools objective.
algorithms.open_source_code: unverified (not found on GitHub search; Fields2Cover repo is the likely host)

notes:
WHAT THE SWEEP FOUND (blunt answer to the critique): our searches turned up no published agricultural CPP that gives a distribution-free / conformal guarantee on missed area. The closest algorithmic competitors are IRIS-U^2 (T-RO 2025, MC statistical guarantees under execution uncertainty, but model-based), PAC coverage (Das-Becker-Bretl 2011), belief-space CPP (Schirmer et al. ICRA 2019), and online track-spacing / sensor-driven coverage (Yordanova & Gips 2020; Paull et al. IROS 2012). The agricultural planners (Fields2Cover RA-L 2023, Hameed RAS 2016 / JIRS 2014 / CEA 2013, H-CCPP JFR 2025, Jin & Tang JFR 2011, Soil2Cover PA 2025) are deterministic and treat GNSS/tracking error with a fixed margin or not at all. The novelty claim holds, but a Q1 paper must compare against these NAMED algorithms, not only margin-rule categories. Minimum set for Q1: F2C, IRIS-U^2-style MC certification, Hameed side-to-side, online pass-to-pass replanning, belief-space lanes; then H-CCPP, PAC, DRL.

HOW TO STOP POINTS COLLAPSING (applies to every competitor): (1) Give each algorithm its native robustness knob (F2C op_width, Hameed+margin, H-CCPP GNSS buffer, PAC delta, IRIS m and beta, belief-space z, online margin m, DRL penalty C). Plot full overlap vs P(no-miss) and overlap vs E[missed] frontier curves, then mark (a) the algorithm's own recommended or default operating point, (b) the oracle point tuned on test data, (c) CE's certified point. CE's selling point is reaching the frontier at the target without test-time tuning, not 'lowest overlap'. (2) Report 'X+CE' for every base planner (F2C, Hameed, H-CCPP, Jin-Tang, online replanning): CE as a planner-agnostic certification layer turns the comparison into planner x margin-rule. (3) Put model-based certifiers (IRIS-U^2, PAC, belief-space) through misspecification (Gaussian vs real heavy-tailed RTK, LOBO/LODO, CitrusFarm real traces vs kinematic model), where they should diverge from CE. (4) Add the 3D footprint projection (w*cos(lateral slope)) to core.evaluate for all methods. Without it, terrain-aware competitors, and CE-A, have nothing to gain on DEM slopes, which may be why CE-U and CE-A coincide. (5) Compute path length and turns for all methods with F2C's DubinsCurvesCC path planner at the vehicle's r_min. Use the same fields, seeds, controllers and metrics throughout.

EXTRA OPEN RESOURCES SEEN: ethz-asl/polygon_coverage_planning (Bähnemann et al., 'Revisiting boustrophedon CPP as a GTSP', FSR 2019; ~670 stars) for route-optimal boustrophedon; Fields2Benchmark (350 vector fields NL/EE/LT, WUR dataset; download reachability unverified); the H-CCPP 30-field 2D/3D dataset (reachability unverified); Oksanen & Visala JFR 26:651-668, 2009 (split-merge trapezoidal decomposition + driving-direction search; covered by F2C's decomposition/brute force).

Unverified: Hameed 2016 DOI; Das et al. venue and DOI; Yordanova & Gips journal venue; H-CCPP volume and pages and its buffer value; Jin & Tang algorithm details; Soil2Cover code location. Verified via GitHub search: Fields2Cover/Fields2Cover, arvijj/rl-cpp, ethz-asl/polygon_coverage_planning. Verified on PyPI: fields2cover 2.1.0 (sdist, downloaded to scratchpad). Needs C++ build with GDAL and OR-tools; fallback is a shapely re-implementation.
